[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday counting starts at 1 and 'up to N' includes N. Java arrays start at index 0 and end at N-1, and a loop with i < N runs N times while i <= N runs N+1 times.
[1] misconception (M) -> OffByOneBound: wrong rule: < and <= (and 0..n versus 0..n-1) are interchangeable in a loop bound. Right rule: i < N runs N times from 0 and i <= N runs N+1 times; with an array of length N only i < N stays inside the indices 0..N-1.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> OffByOneBound: Applies the bound rule unevenly: writes i < a.length in one loop and i <= a.length in the next one over the same array. (here mixing in: "< vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable")

[0] names_the_element (N): Off-by-one error: a loop or index that is one step too far or too short.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Indices run from 0 to N-1; a loop for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) runs exactly N times. Misunderstanding the 0-based convention leads to off-by-one errors, which are hard to avoid and debug.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: to check a bound, trace the first pass (the start value) and the last pass (the value that makes the condition false), not only a middle pass.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) gives i = 0..4, five passes; i <= 5 gives six passes, and a[5] on an array of length 5 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one extra pass reads or writes one element past the end (an exception) or adds one term too many; one missing pass leaves the last element unprocessed.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Because indexing starts at 0, the last valid index is length-1, and that is the bound most often missed by one.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): The start value and the condition together fix the number of passes; changing either by one changes the count by one.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): When one action must happen once more (or less) than the other, the fencepost plan handles the extra case explicitly instead of risking an off-by-one.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: choose the bounds from the meaning (count N things, valid indices 0..N-1) and check the first and last pass, rather than guessing.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> OffByOneBound: Conservation: changing < to <= adds exactly one pass; starting at 1 instead of 0 removes exactly one; both keep the loop otherwise the same.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count. Kind: see node. Trigger class: see node
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Whenever writing a loop over a range or an array, write the bound from the count (i < N for N passes from 0) and check the first and last values of the index by hand.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A traversal of an array of length N must use indices 0..N-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: i <= a.length, a[i+1] on the last pass, or a[i-1] at i = 0 (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A loop meant to run N times must run exactly N times. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: the loop stops one short or goes one too far, so the last element is skipped or one term too many is added

An off-by-one error is a loop that runs once too many or too few; a fencepost loop is the correct plan for the case that needs one action more than the other.
Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
The initialization and the condition of a loop fix how many times it runs; one wrong bound makes it run once too many or too few.
